select.title: Free mission
select.subtitle: Any scenario, no career progress. Every choice moves mass, power, data, budget, schedule and lifetime — and there is never just one right answer.
select.step1: Read the briefing: goal, budget, deadline and requirements.
select.step2: Pick instruments in **Payload**; watch the resource meters on the right react.
select.step3: Tune the spacecraft, orbit, launcher and ground stations until nothing is red.
select.step4: Open **Review**: every warning explains why, and what you could change.
design.spacecraftTitle: Your spacecraft: every part you choose appears here, on the launch pad and in flight.
design.spacecraftDesc: Built from your choices: arrays, antenna, instruments (green = astrobiology, violet = astrophysics), thrusters and radiators.

payload.cargo.hint: Food, water, experiments and spare parts for the station crew. You are paid per kilogram delivered — but every kilogram must be launched.
payload.instruments.hint: Pick what your mission carries. Each instrument adds mass, power, data and cost. Stars = how useful it is for this scenario. Duty cycle = share of the day it is switched on.
comms.band.hint: Higher bands carry more data but cost more power and money. Link rate here: {rate} Mbit/s (band × antenna gain × distance factor).
comms.stations.hint: Contact: {contact} min/day → {downlink} GB/day. Each station adds a monthly fee. Polar orbits pass over high-latitude stations on almost every orbit.
comms.storage.fillsIn: At current rates it fills in {days} days.

review.hint: Automatic checklist. Red = blocking (cannot launch). Amber = allowed but risky or costly. Green = healthy. Each item explains why and what you can change.
review.status.errors: Red items would make the mission impossible.
review.status.warnings: Amber items are allowed — but the mission will feel them.
orbit.title: Orbit
orbit.hint: Where you fly decides eclipses, contact time, radiation, how much the launcher can carry and how much Δv you must bring.
orbit.dragHint: Lower altitude = sharper images and shorter passes, but more air drag (more propellant to stay up).
orbit.route.title: Route — the three-body problem
orbit.route.hint: Between the Earth and the Moon three bodies pull on your spacecraft. Faster routes cost propellant; slow “low-energy” routes let gravity do the work but cross chaotic regions where small errors grow.
orbit.route.tcmFormat: {val} m/s (expected need ~{need}; what is left at arrival funds station-keeping)
orbit.cr3bp.label: Route to the L2 orbit
orbit.cr3bp.legend: Yellow: real periodic orbit computed in the game (planar version of a halo). Blue dashed: schematic route.
orbit.launcher.title: Launcher
orbit.launcher.hint: Capacity shown for your chosen orbit. Your fully fuelled spacecraft must fit.
orbit.launcher.unlockHint: Unlock it in your career’s technology tree.
spacecraft.arrays.title: Power — solar arrays
spacecraft.arrays.hint: Generation: P = area × efficiency × 1361 W/m² × cos(angle to Sun), only while in sunlight. Panels lose a few % per year.
spacecraft.battery.title: Power — battery
spacecraft.battery.hint: Carries the spacecraft through eclipses. Using a big share of it every orbit wears it out.
spacecraft.battery.chartTitle: One orbit ({min} min): solar vs load and battery charge
spacecraft.adcs.title: Attitude control (ADCS)
spacecraft.adcs.hint: How precisely the spacecraft can point. Sharp cameras and dishes need better pointing.
spacecraft.obc.title: On-board computer
spacecraft.obc.hint: Stores data between ground passes. Radiation slowly damages ordinary electronics.
spacecraft.compression.title: Data compression
spacecraft.compression.hint: Squeezes data before download. Lossy compression throws away some detail.
spacecraft.propulsion.title: Propulsion
spacecraft.propulsion.hint: Rocket equation: Δv = Isp × g₀ × ln(wet/dry). This mission needs {dv} m/s → {prop} kg of propellant.
spacecraft.thermal.title: Thermal control
spacecraft.life.title: Design life
spacecraft.life.hint: Propellant and operations are sized for this. Longer life = more propellant, more operations cost, more science.
dashboard.mass.label: Mass (wet / launcher)
dashboard.mass.tip: Wet mass = parts + 22% structure + 20% design margin + tanks + propellant (rocket equation). Must fit the launcher's capacity to this orbit.
dashboard.power.label: Power (need / generated EOL)
dashboard.power.tip: Orbit-average generation P = A·η·1361 W/m²·cosθ·(1−eclipse), degraded each year. Need = average load incl. battery recharge losses.
dashboard.dod.label: Battery depth of discharge
dashboard.dod.tip: Share of the battery used in each eclipse. Many deep cycles per year wear the battery out.
dashboard.data.label: Data (produced / downlink per day)
dashboard.data.tip: Produced = Σ rate × duty cycle ÷ compression. Downlink = contact minutes × link rate × 70% efficiency.
dashboard.budget.label: Budget
dashboard.budget.tip: Instruments (× TRL factor) + bus + integration + launcher + operations, plus 15% contingency.
dashboard.schedule.label: Development time
dashboard.schedule.tip: 18 months base + extra for low-TRL items + 1.5 per extra instrument + 1 per 100 kg.
dashboard.life.label: Lifetime (limit: {factor})
dashboard.life.tip: Life = min(battery, panels, propellant/plan, radiation, orbit). The smallest one ends the mission.
dashboard.science.tip: Expected science points per year (value × relevance × data actually delivered).
dashboard.science.label: Science / year
dashboard.risk.tip: Launcher reliability × bus × instruments (by TRL) × environmental risks.
dashboard.risk.label: Success chance

firstLight.title: Prologue — First Light
firstLight.desc: In a workshop in Arequipa, {director} rebuilt the liquid-propellant rocket described in Pedro Paulet’s notebooks. Investors will only listen once it reaches space — the 100 km line — with a real experiment on board.
firstLight.tooHeavy: — too heavy! A small rocket cannot carry both.
firstLight.lesson: Lesson: reaching space is about going **up** 100 km; staying there is about going **sideways** at ~7.8 km/s — about five times faster than Paulet-1.
learn.title: Learn
learn.orbit.diagram: Newton’s cannon (to scale): fired sideways from 200 km
learn.orbit.falls: Too slow: the ground curves away less than you fall, so you hit the Earth.
learn.orbit.escape: Faster than ~11.2 km/s: you escape Earth’s gravity for good.
learn.orbit.orbit: About 7.8 km/s: you fall around the Earth forever — that is an orbit!
learn.orbit.stretched: Between orbital and escape speed: a stretched orbit (an ellipse).
learn.orbit.explanation: An orbit is not “floating”: the spacecraft is always falling, but moving sideways so fast that the Earth curves away beneath it. Lower orbits are faster (~7.7 km/s at 400 km); geostationary satellites move at ~3.1 km/s and take 24 h per lap.
learn.rocket.mark.leo: Low Earth orbit (incl. ~1.5 km/s gravity & drag losses)
learn.rocket.explanation: Δv grows only with the logarithm of the mass ratio: doubling the propellant does not double your speed. That is why rockets drop empty stages (staging), why efficient engines matter, and why landing a booster for reuse costs payload — the landing propellant is mass you could have used to go faster.
learn.chaos.changeSpeed: Change in the starting speed of the second spacecraft:
learn.chaos.viewLabel: Two almost identical spacecraft near L2
learn.chaos.distTitle: Distance between the two spacecraft (log scale: 1 km → 1 000 000 km)
learn.chaos.diverged: After {days} days the two spacecraft are already 1 000 km apart — although their speeds differed by about {diff} cm/s at the start.
learn.chaos.stayClose: In this time they stay close… try more days or a bigger change.
learn.chaos.p1.title: This is chaos.
learn.chaos.p1.body: The motion is perfectly deterministic — the same starting numbers give exactly the same path, every time, in every browser (the game guarantees it). But near the Lagrange points tiny differences grow exponentially, so any small navigation error soon becomes a big one. Henri Poincaré found this behaviour while studying the three-body problem around 1890. Look at the yellow “perfect” orbit too: after a few loops even it slides away — the orbit is unstable, and the tiniest rounding error is enough.
learn.chaos.p2.title: Why it matters:
learn.chaos.p2.body: spacecraft on halo orbits make small, regular correction burns — cheap if done early, expensive if you wait. The same chaos is also a gift: low-energy routes use it to reach the Moon or L2 with very little propellant.
learn.chaos.p3: In the game: Cadets watch this lesson, Researchers choose between precomputed routes, Program Directors also size the correction reserve and decide when to correct.
learn.budgets.mass.title: Mass
learn.budgets.mass.desc: Every kilogram must be lifted. Parts + ~22% structure + a 20% safety margin + propellant from the rocket equation must fit the launcher.
learn.budgets.power.title: Power
learn.budgets.power.desc: Solar panels only work in sunlight. During eclipses the battery carries the load — and every deep discharge ages it.
learn.budgets.data.title: Data
learn.budgets.data.desc: Instruments produce more data than radios can send. Ground passes last minutes; more stations or faster bands open the bottleneck.
learn.budgets.money.title: Money & time
learn.budgets.money.desc: Immature (low-TRL) technology costs more and takes longer. Investors fund results, not dreams.
learn.budgets.tradeoff: In the game, change any part and watch all four budgets move at once — that coupling is what spacecraft engineers call a trade-off.
learn.paulet.fact.documented: Pedro Paulet was born in Arequipa, Peru, in 1874 and died in Buenos Aires in 1945. He studied in Paris and worked as an engineer.
learn.paulet.fact.account: In a letter published in the Lima newspaper El Comercio in 1927, he said that around 1895–1897 in Paris he had tested a rocket engine burning liquid propellants.
learn.paulet.fact.disputed: No independent record of those tests has been found; later historians could not verify them. Treat them as his claim, not established fact.
learn.paulet.fact.comparison: The first verified flight of a liquid-propellant rocket was Robert Goddard’s, in Massachusetts, in 1926.
learn.paulet.fact.inGame: {director} (fictional) builds Paulet-1 from those ideas. It reaches space but cannot reach orbit.

role.lead.blurb: Principal Investigator: contract, investors, budget, launcher, ground stations, schedule, final sign-off.
role.engineer.blurb: Builds the spacecraft: power, propulsion, structure, thermal, computer, radio and antenna.
role.astrophysicist.blurb: Orbits and trajectories, space weather, telescopes, radar and particle instruments.
role.astrobiologist.blurb: Water, life and habitability; Earth-system and planetary science; spectrometers and imagers.
glossary.dv: How much the spacecraft can change its speed with its own engine. Every manoeuvre costs Δv, and Δv costs propellant (rocket equation).
glossary.dutyCycle: Fraction of the day an instrument is switched on. More time on = more data and power use.
glossary.eclipse: Time when the planet blocks the Sun. Solar panels give nothing; the battery must carry the load.
glossary.dod: How much of the battery you use per eclipse. Deep cycles wear batteries out faster.
glossary.trl: Technology Readiness Level (6–9). 9 = flown many times; 6 = prototype. Lower TRL costs more, takes longer and fails more often.
glossary.linkBudget: How much data per second a radio link can carry; depends on band, antenna and distance.
glossary.payloadCapacity: Maximum mass a launcher can deliver to a given orbit.
glossary.isp: Fuel efficiency of an engine, in seconds. Higher Isp = more Δv per kg of propellant.
lifeFactor.battery: the battery wearing out from charge cycles
lifeFactor.panels: solar panels degrading below what you need
lifeFactor.propellant: the planned mission life (propellant and operations are sized for it)
lifeFactor.orbit: the orbit decaying with no thrusters to correct it
review.msg.NO_PAYLOAD.title: No instruments on board
review.msg.NO_PAYLOAD.why: A spacecraft without instruments returns no science. Open the Payload tab and add at least one instrument.
review.msg.NO_PAYLOAD.lever.0: Payload tab → add an instrument the scenario needs
review.msg.MASS_OVER_CAPACITY.title: Too heavy for the launcher
review.msg.MASS_OVER_CAPACITY.why: Your spacecraft weighs {wet} kg fully fuelled, but the {launcher} can only carry {capacity} kg to this orbit. It would never reach orbit.
review.msg.MASS_MARGIN_LOW.title: Launcher almost full
review.msg.MASS_MARGIN_LOW.why: You use {wet} of {capacity} kg. Real spacecraft tend to grow during development; less than 10 % spare capacity is risky.
review.msg.MASS_MARGIN_LOW.lever.1: Pick a launcher with more capacity
review.msg.LAUNCHER_NO_TARGET.title: Launcher cannot reach this orbit
review.msg.LAUNCHER_NO_TARGET.why: The {launcher} is not powerful enough to send anything towards {orbit}.
review.msg.LAUNCHER_OVERSIZED.title: You are paying for unused rocket
review.msg.LAUNCHER_OVERSIZED.why: The {cheaper} could carry this spacecraft and would save about ${saving} M compared with the {launcher}.
review.msg.LAUNCHER_OVERSIZED.lever.1: Or use the spare capacity for more payload
review.msg.NO_PROPULSION_INSERTION.title: No engine to finish the trip
review.msg.NO_PROPULSION_INSERTION.why: The launcher drops you on a transfer path; reaching {orbit} needs another {dv} m/s that only the spacecraft's own engine can provide.
review.msg.DV_INFEASIBLE.title: This engine cannot do the job
review.msg.DV_INFEASIBLE.why: You need {dv} m/s of Δv but an engine with Isp {isp} s would need more propellant than any tank can hold (rocket equation).
review.msg.DV_INFEASIBLE.lever.0: Use propulsion with higher Isp (hydrazine, electric)
review.msg.POWER_NEGATIVE.title: Not enough power
review.msg.POWER_NEGATIVE.why: Your solar arrays deliver {gen} W on average over an orbit, but the spacecraft needs {need} W (including recharging the battery for eclipse). The battery would drain and the spacecraft would shut down — like a phone that uses more than its charger gives.
review.msg.POWER_EOL_NEGATIVE.title: Power runs short before end of mission
review.msg.POWER_EOL_NEGATIVE.why: Panels degrade every year. After {years} years they give only {gen} W vs {need} W needed.
review.msg.POWER_MARGIN_LOW.title: Thin power margin
review.msg.POWER_MARGIN_LOW.why: End-of-life power margin is only {marginPct} %. Engineers usually keep 10–25 % for surprises.
review.msg.POWER_OVERSIZED.title: Solar arrays bigger than needed
review.msg.POWER_OVERSIZED.why: You have {marginPct} % more power than needed even at end of life. That extra area costs mass and money.
review.msg.POWER_OVERSIZED.lever.1: Or use the spare power for more instruments
review.msg.BATTERY_DEPLETED.title: Battery dies in every eclipse
review.msg.BATTERY_DEPLETED.why: Each eclipse lasts {eclipseMin} min and needs {need} Wh, but the battery holds only {have} Wh.
review.msg.BATTERY_DOD_HIGH.title: Battery discharged too deeply
review.msg.BATTERY_DOD_HIGH.why: Each eclipse empties {dodPct} % of the battery. With ~{cycles} eclipses per year, staying above {limitPct} % depth of discharge wears it out quickly (shorter life).
review.msg.BATTERY_WORST_CASE.title: Cannot run everything during eclipse
review.msg.BATTERY_WORST_CASE.why: With all instruments and the radio on ({peak} W) for a full {eclipseMin} min eclipse, the {have} Wh battery would run flat. Operations will have to schedule instruments.
review.msg.LONG_ECLIPSE_RISK.title: May not survive a long eclipse
review.msg.LONG_ECLIPSE_RISK.why: Occasionally the Earth's shadow covers the Moon for ~{hours} h. Even in safe mode you would need {need} Wh but the battery holds {have} Wh.
review.msg.ELECTRIC_UNDERPOWERED.title: Electric thruster starved of power
review.msg.ELECTRIC_UNDERPOWERED.why: Electric propulsion needs about {need} W in sunlight while thrusting; your arrays give {have} W.
review.msg.NO_STATIONS.title: No ground stations
review.msg.NO_STATIONS.why: Without a ground station nobody can receive your data or send commands.
review.msg.NO_STATIONS.lever.0: Ground & Comms → select at least one station
review.msg.NO_DEEP_STATION.title: Too far for ordinary antennas
review.msg.NO_DEEP_STATION.why: From {orbit} the signal is extremely weak. Only large deep-space antennas can hear it.
review.msg.NO_DEEP_STATION.lever.0: Select at least one Deep Space Antenna
review.msg.DATA_BOTTLENECK.title: Data bottleneck
review.msg.DATA_BOTTLENECK.why: Your instruments produce {generated} GB/day but you can only download {downlink} GB/day. The on-board memory ({storage} GB) fills in {daysToFull} days; after that {lostPct} % of the data is lost.
review.msg.DATA_BOTTLENECK.lever.0: Add another ground station (high-latitude ones see polar orbits more often)
review.msg.DATA_BOTTLENECK.lever.1: Use a higher band (X → Ka) or a bigger antenna
review.msg.ANTENNA_INCOMPATIBLE.title: Antenna does not fit this radio
review.msg.ANTENNA_INCOMPATIBLE.why: The {antenna} antenna cannot be used with {band}.
review.msg.DISH_NEEDS_POINTING.title: Dish cannot be aimed
review.msg.DISH_NEEDS_POINTING.why: A steerable dish needs accurate attitude control; with {adcs} it misses Earth often and the data rate drops.
review.msg.DISH_NEEDS_POINTING.lever.0: Use reaction wheels or a star tracker
review.msg.MAGNETORQUERS_NO_FIELD.title: Magnetorquers need a magnetic field
review.msg.MAGNETORQUERS_NO_FIELD.why: Magnetorquers push against Earth’s magnetic field. Far from Earth there is no field to push against: the spacecraft would tumble.
Use reaction wheels or a star tracker
review.msg.POINTING_INSUFFICIENT.title: {instrument} needs precise pointing
review.msg.POINTING_INSUFFICIENT.why: This instrument needs {need} pointing; {have} cannot hold it steady enough, so it would return blurred, useless data.
review.msg.POINTING_DEGRADED.title: {instrument} works poorly
review.msg.POINTING_DEGRADED.why: It needs {need} pointing; with {have} you get about half the science.
review.msg.LOW_SUN_OPTICAL.title: Long shadows for optical cameras
review.msg.LOW_SUN_OPTICAL.why: In a dawn-dusk orbit the ground below is at sunrise or sunset. Optical cameras get dark, shadowed images (half the science). Radar does not care.
review.msg.LOW_SUN_OPTICAL.lever.0: Use the 10:30 sun-synchronous orbit for optical instruments
review.msg.COLD_RISK.title: Risk of freezing
review.msg.COLD_RISK.why: Around {orbit} long cold periods can freeze batteries and propellant lines without heaters.
review.msg.DEBRIS_NO_DISPOSAL.title: Cannot clean up after itself
review.msg.DEBRIS_NO_DISPOSAL.why: Without thrusters you cannot lower the orbit ({dv} m/s) at end of life; the dead satellite stays as space debris for decades.
review.msg.LIFE_SHORT.title: Mission ends too early
review.msg.LIFE_SHORT.why: Expected life is {life} years but {required} are required. The limit is {factor}.
review.msg.LIFE_SHORT.lever.0: Fix the limiting factor shown in the Lifetime panel
review.msg.RADIATION.title: Computer may not survive the radiation
review.msg.RADIATION.why: This orbit gives ~{dose} krad per year; the {obc} tolerates it for ~{years} years.
review.msg.OVER_BUDGET.title: Over budget
review.msg.OVER_BUDGET.why: The mission costs ${total} M but the budget is ${budget} M. The agency will not approve it.
review.msg.OVER_BUDGET.lever.1: Fewer or more mature (higher TRL) instruments
review.msg.BUDGET_TIGHT.title: Budget almost exhausted
review.msg.BUDGET_TIGHT.why: ${total} M of ${budget} M used. Any surprise will push you over.
review.msg.LATE.title: Development will run late
review.msg.LATE.why: Building this spacecraft takes ~{months} months but launch is planned in {deadline}. Immature instruments (low TRL) and heavy designs take longer.
review.msg.LAUNCHER_SUBORBITAL.title: {launcher} cannot reach orbit
review.msg.LAUNCHER_SUBORBITAL.why: It is a sounding rocket: it climbs to ~{apogee} km for a few minutes and falls back. Staying in orbit needs ~7.8 km/s of sideways speed; Paulet-1 reaches about 1.5 km/s straight up.
review.msg.LAUNCHER_SUBORBITAL.lever.0: Choose an orbital launcher (unlocked after First Light in the campaign)
review.msg.RIDESHARE_ALTITUDE.title: The rideshare does not go that high
review.msg.RIDESHARE_ALTITUDE.why: Shared flights drop everyone at the same place (up to ~{max} km). You asked for {alt} km.
review.msg.RIDESHARE_ALTITUDE.lever.0: Lower the altitude to {max} km or less
review.msg.RIDESHARE_SCHEDULE.title: Waiting for the next shared flight
review.msg.RIDESHARE_SCHEDULE.why: Rideshares fly every {every} months; your satellite waits ~{wait} months on the ground after it is ready.
review.msg.RIDESHARE_SCHEDULE.lever.1: Or pay for a dedicated launcher to fly as soon as you are ready
review.msg.TCM_RESERVE_LOW.title: Small correction reserve for a chaotic route
review.msg.TCM_RESERVE_LOW.why: On the {route} small navigation errors grow quickly (chaos). Expected corrections are ~{need} m/s but you carry {reserve} m/s.
review.msg.TCM_RESERVE_LOW.lever.1: Pick a faster, less sensitive route
review.msg.MASS_OK.title: Mass fits the launcher
review.msg.MASS_OK.why: Fully fuelled mass is within launcher capacity with a healthy margin.
review.msg.POWER_OK.title: Power balance positive
review.msg.POWER_OK.why: Arrays cover all loads, including battery recharge, through end of life.
review.msg.DATA_OK.title: Downlink keeps up
review.msg.DATA_OK.why: Everything your instruments produce can be downloaded each day.
review.msg.COST_OK.title: Within budget
review.msg.COST_OK.why: Total cost, including 15 % contingency, fits the budget.
review.msg.SCHEDULE_OK.title: On schedule
review.msg.SCHEDULE_OK.why: Development fits before the planned launch date.
review.msg.LIFE_OK.title: Lifetime meets the requirement
review.msg.LIFE_OK.why: Battery, panels, propellant, radiation tolerance and orbit all last long enough.
review.msg.SCIENCE_OK.title: Payload ready
review.msg.SCIENCE_OK.why: Instruments have the pointing and lighting they need.
cause.CAUSE_LAUNCH_FAILURE.title: The rocket failed
cause.CAUSE_LAUNCH_FAILURE.why: Your launcher succeeds about {reliability}% of the time. This time it did not. Bad luck — but a real risk you chose.
cause.CAUSE_LAUNCH_FAILURE.change: Fly again with a new seed, or pay for a more reliable launcher.
cause.CAUSE_END_BATTERY.title: Battery wore out early
cause.CAUSE_END_BATTERY.why: The battery died after {life} years (needed {required}). Deep discharges in thousands of eclipses age it fast.
cause.CAUSE_END_BATTERY.change: Use a bigger battery so each eclipse drains less of it.
cause.CAUSE_END_POWER.title: Not enough power at the end
cause.CAUSE_END_POWER.why: Solar arrays degraded until they could not run the spacecraft (after {life} years).
cause.CAUSE_END_POWER.change: Add array area margin for end of life.
cause.CAUSE_END_RADIATION.title: Radiation killed the computer
cause.CAUSE_END_RADIATION.why: The computer exceeded its radiation tolerance after {life} years.
cause.CAUSE_END_RADIATION.change: Use a radiation-hardened computer or a gentler orbit.
cause.CAUSE_END_ORBIT.title: Could not keep the orbit
cause.CAUSE_END_ORBIT.why: Without enough propellant or thrusters, the orbit decayed after {life} years.
cause.CAUSE_END_ORBIT.change: Carry propulsion and size propellant for the whole mission.
cause.CAUSE_END_FUNDING.title: The money ran out
cause.CAUSE_END_FUNDING.why: Investors stopped paying for operations after {life} years. Society’s rules apply in space too.
cause.CAUSE_END_FUNDING.change: Keep a larger budget reserve or cheaper operations (fewer stations).
cause.CAUSE_END_COLLISION.title: Lost to space debris
cause.CAUSE_END_COLLISION.why: You accepted a collision risk and lost the bet.
cause.CAUSE_END_COLLISION.change: Carry propellant for avoidance manoeuvres and use it.
cause.CAUSE_END_ECLIPSE.title: Frozen in a lunar eclipse
cause.CAUSE_END_ECLIPSE.why: The battery could not carry the spacecraft through hours of Earth’s shadow.
cause.CAUSE_END_ECLIPSE.change: Size the battery for the long eclipse, or power down before it.
cause.CAUSE_DATA_LOST.title: Data was lost
cause.CAUSE_DATA_LOST.why: {lostPct}% of everything your instruments produced never reached the ground.
cause.CAUSE_DATA_LOST.change: More ground stations, a faster radio, lower duty cycles or compression.
cause.CAUSE_BOTTLENECK.title: Downlink bottleneck
cause.CAUSE_BOTTLENECK.why: Instruments produced {gen} GB/day but only {down} GB/day could be downloaded.
cause.CAUSE_BOTTLENECK.change: Add a high-latitude station or a higher band.
cause.CAUSE_SAFE_MODE.title: Too much time in safe mode
cause.CAUSE_SAFE_MODE.why: {weeks} weeks without science after flares, anomalies or eclipses.
cause.CAUSE_SAFE_MODE.change: Radiation-hardened electronics and battery margin reduce downtime.
cause.CAUSE_MISSED_OPPORTUNITY.title: Missed a science opportunity
cause.CAUSE_MISSED_OPPORTUNITY.why: “{title}” happened {count} time(s) and no instrument on board could observe it.
cause.CAUSE_MISSED_OPPORTUNITY.change: Fly an instrument that fits the scenario’s surprises.
cause.CAUSE_SEIZED_OPPORTUNITY.title: Seized a science opportunity
cause.CAUSE_POOR_DECISIONS.title: Risky calls in flight
cause.CAUSE_POOR_DECISIONS.why: {count} decision(s) took more risk than the situation justified.
cause.CAUSE_POOR_DECISIONS.change: Read what each role is worried about before choosing.
cause.CAUSE_GOOD_DECISIONS.title: Sound decisions under pressure
cause.CAUSE_OVER_BUDGET.title: Over budget
cause.CAUSE_OVER_BUDGET.why: Final cost ${cost} M vs budget ${budget} M.
cause.CAUSE_OVER_BUDGET.change: Cheaper launcher, fewer stations or more mature instruments.
cause.CAUSE_LATE.title: Launched late
cause.CAUSE_LATE.whyWithDelay: {months} months behind schedule (including a {delay}-month launcher delay).
cause.CAUSE_LATE.change: Higher-TRL instruments and a lighter spacecraft develop faster.
cause.CAUSE_COMPLETED.title: Mission completed
cause.CAUSE_COMPLETED.why: The spacecraft operated for {life} years as planned.
cause.CAUSE_BOOSTER_LANDED.title: The booster came home
cause.CAUSE_BOOSTER_LANDED.why: Your reusable first stage landed and can fly again — cheaper launches and prestige.
cause.CAUSE_BOOSTER_LOST.title: Booster lost at sea
cause.CAUSE_BOOSTER_LOST.why: The reusable first stage missed its landing. The mission was fine, but replacing the booster costs money.
cause.CAUSE_BOOSTER_LOST.change: Landings get more reliable with experience; it is still worth it on average.
cause.CAUSE_STRONG_DOWNLINK.title: Plenty of downlink
cause.CAUSE_STRONG_DOWNLINK.why: {down} GB/day of capacity kept data flowing even during outages.
cause.CAUSE_LOW_SCIENCE.title: Science fell short
cause.CAUSE_LOW_SCIENCE.why: {science} science points against a target of {target}.
cause.CAUSE_LOW_SCIENCE.change: More relevant instruments (stars in Payload), higher duty cycles if downlink allows.
protagonist.bio: Physicist from Arequipa, Peru. Inspired as a kid by the story of Pedro Paulet, now Mission Director (Principal Investigator) of a small space institute.
component.pan_camera.name: Panchromatic Camera
component.pan_camera.description: Black-and-white imager. Cheap, proven, sharp shapes but no colour information.
component.multispectral.name: Multispectral Imager
component.multispectral.description: Sees several colour bands (incl. near-infrared) — the workhorse for crops and forests.
component.sar.name: Synthetic Aperture Radar
component.sar.description: Active radar that images through clouds and at night. Power and data hungry.
component.ir_spectrometer.name: Infrared Spectrometer
component.ir_spectrometer.description: Splits infrared light to identify minerals, water and plant stress.
component.magnetometer.name: Magnetometer
component.magnetometer.description: Measures magnetic fields. Tiny, cheap, always on.
component.laser_altimeter.name: Laser Altimeter
component.laser_altimeter.description: Fires laser pulses to map terrain height and shadowed craters.
component.particle_detector.name: Particle Detector
component.particle_detector.description: Counts energetic particles: space weather and radiation environment.
component.hires_camera.name: High-Resolution Camera
component.hires_camera.description: Telescope-class camera. Needs very stable pointing and a fat downlink.
component.hyperspectral.name: Hyperspectral Imager
component.hyperspectral.description: Hundreds of narrow colour bands: crop type, water quality, soil chemistry.
component.neutron_spectrometer.name: Neutron Spectrometer
component.neutron_spectrometer.descripti: Detects hydrogen (a hint of water ice) from orbit by counting neutrons.
component.thermal_ir.name: Thermal Infrared Camera
component.thermal_ir.description: Sees heat: fires, drought stress, cold traps.
component.mw_radiometer.name: Microwave Radiometer
component.mw_radiometer.description: Measures soil moisture, rain and ice through clouds.
component.ir_telescope.name: Infrared Space Telescope
component.ir_telescope.description: A cooled infrared telescope: sees young galaxies and dusty star nurseries. Needs a cold, stable, eclipse-free spot.
component.radio_array.name: Low-Frequency Radio Antennas
component.radio_array.description: Listens to the faint radio hiss of the early Universe — only possible where the Moon blocks Earth’s radio noise.
component.weather_imager.name: Wide-Field Weather Imager
component.weather_imager.description: Watches whole cloud systems evolve. Best from high orbits.
component.leo.name: Low Earth Orbit (51.6°)
component.leo.description: Close to Earth: sharp images and cheap launches, but air drag, frequent eclipses and short ground passes. Does not fly over the poles.
component.sso.name: Sun-Synchronous Orbit (10:30)
component.sso.description: Polar orbit that crosses each place at the same local time (mid-morning): consistent lighting, ideal for Earth observation. Eclipses every orbit.
component.sso_dd.name: Dawn-Dusk Sun-Synchronous
component.sso_dd.description: Rides the day/night line: almost permanent sunlight (small battery!), but the ground below is at sunrise/sunset, so optical cameras see long shadows.
component.meo.name: Medium Earth Orbit
component.meo.description: Navigation-satellite altitude: ~12 h period and long passes, but inside the radiation belts.
component.geo.name: Geostationary Orbit
component.geo.description: Hovers over one spot on the equator: permanent contact and continuous view of a hemisphere, but far away and costly to reach.
component.lunar_polar.name: Low Lunar Polar Orbit
component.lunar_polar.description: Passes over both lunar poles every ~2 h. Needs a braking burn to be captured, regular corrections (lumpy gravity), and deep-space antennas on Earth.
component.em_l2_halo.name: Earth–Moon L2 halo orbit
component.em_l2_halo.description: A loop around the L2 point, ~64 500 km beyond the Moon, where Earth’s and the Moon’s pull balance the spacecraft’s motion. Almost no eclipses and a radio-quiet view — but the orbit is unstable (chaos): it needs regular small corrections.
component.helio.name: Heliocentric (Mars flyby)
component.helio.description: Leaves Earth for good. Weaker sunlight, tiny data rates, minutes of signal delay, years of cruise.
component.paulet.name: Paulet-1 (sounding rocket)
component.paulet.realWorld: Built by Pedro Goicochea from Pedro Paulet’s notebooks (fiction). Paulet claimed in a 1927 letter to have tested a liquid-propellant engine in Paris in the 1890s — not independently verified. The first verified liquid-fuel rocket flight was Robert Goddard’s, in 1926.
component.light.name: Light (L-1)
component.light.realWorld: Small dedicated launchers (a few hundred kg to low orbit) appeared in the late 2010s for small satellites.
component.rideshare.name: Rideshare (shared ride to SSO)
component.rideshare.realWorld: Dedicated rideshare flights carry dozens of small satellites at once to sun-synchronous orbit: cheap per kg, but you go when and where the rocket goes.
component.medium.name: Medium (M-2)
component.medium.realWorld: Classic medium launchers, thrown away after each flight, flew most satellites of the last decades.
component.reusable_medium.name: R-2 Reusable Medium
component.reusable_medium.realWorld: In December 2015 an orbital rocket’s first stage (Falcon 9) landed back for the first time; boosters have been re-flown since 2017. Landing needs propellant, so a reusable rocket lifts less than the same rocket thrown away — but each flight costs much less.
component.reusable_heavy.name: R-3 Reusable Heavy
component.reusable_heavy.realWorld: In 2018 the two side boosters of a heavy rocket (Falcon Heavy) landed side by side after launch. Recovering three cores makes heavy launches much cheaper.
component.heavy.name: Heavy (H-3)
component.heavy.realWorld: Heavy expendable launchers send big satellites to geostationary orbit and probes to the Moon and planets.
component.body.name: Body-mounted panels
component.body.description: Cells glued to the spacecraft body. Simple and light, but rarely face the Sun squarely.
component.deployable.name: Deployable fixed wings
component.deployable.description: Wings that unfold after launch. More area, better angle.
component.tracking.name: Sun-tracking wings
component.tracking.description: Motorised wings that follow the Sun. Most power per m², heavier and pricier.

component.wheels.name: Reaction wheels

component.none.name: None
component.none.description: No thrusters: lighter and cheaper, but you cannot change or keep your orbit.
component.coldgas.name: Cold gas
component.coldgas.description: Compressed gas through a nozzle. Simple and safe, very inefficient.
component.hydrazine.name: Hydrazine monopropellant
component.hydrazine.description: The classic satellite thruster: decent efficiency, toxic fuel, needs heaters.
component.electric.name: Electric (ion/Hall)
component.electric.description: Extremely efficient but gentle: needs ~600 W while thrusting and months to change orbit.

scenario.earth_watch.name: Earth Watch
scenario.earth_watch.tagline: Watch forests and farms from orbit for two years.
scenario.earth_watch.objective: Build a satellite that images forests and farmland every few days for at least 2 years, and gets at least 15 GB of imagery to the ground every day.
scenario.earth_watch.whyItMatters: Earth-observation satellites help track deforestation, droughts and harvests; many of them fly in sun-synchronous orbits for consistent lighting.
scenario.lunar_pathfinder.name: Lunar Pathfinder
scenario.lunar_pathfinder.tagline: Hunt for water ice at the lunar poles.
scenario.lunar_pathfinder.objective: Reach a low polar orbit around the Moon and map the permanently shadowed craters for at least 1 year, delivering at least 3 GB of data per day.
scenario.lunar_pathfinder.whyItMatters: Water ice in shadowed polar craters could one day supply drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel for explorers; several orbiters have searched for it.
scenario.andean_eye.name: Andean Eye
scenario.andean_eye.tagline: Watch Andean glaciers and the edge of the Amazon.
scenario.andean_eye.objective: A foundation wants a small satellite that tracks retreating Andean glaciers and the forest edge of the Amazon for at least 3 years, delivering at least 8 GB of images per day — on a tight budget.
scenario.andean_eye.whyItMatters: Tropical glaciers supply water to millions of people in the Andes and are shrinking fast; satellites are the practical way to monitor remote ice and forests.
scenario.storm_tracker.name: Storm Tracker
scenario.storm_tracker.tagline: Watch hurricanes form, from 36 000 km up.
scenario.storm_tracker.objective: A weather agency needs a geostationary satellite that watches storms over the Atlantic continuously for at least 5 years and delivers at least 30 GB of data per day.
scenario.storm_tracker.whyItMatters: Geostationary weather satellites stare at the same hemisphere all the time, which is how forecasters follow a hurricane from birth to landfall.
scenario.station_resupply.name: Station Resupply
scenario.station_resupply.tagline: Deliver a tonne of supplies to the space station.
scenario.station_resupply.objective: A commercial partner pays per kilogram delivered: carry at least 1 000 kg of cargo to the space station (about 420 km, 51.6°) with a cargo spacecraft that can manoeuvre to rendezvous.
scenario.station_resupply.whyItMatters: Since the 2010s commercial cargo spacecraft have kept the International Space Station supplied with food, experiments and spare parts.
scenario.lagrange_observatory.name: Lagrange Observatory
scenario.lagrange_observatory.tagline: A telescope in the quiet, chaotic dark beyond the Moon.
scenario.lagrange_observatory.objective: Place a telescope on a halo orbit around the Earth–Moon L2 point for at least 3 years and send home at least 2 GB per day. The orbit is unstable: plan your route and your correction reserve.
scenario.lagrange_observatory.whyItMatte: Lagrange-point orbits give telescopes a stable thermal environment and few eclipses; behind the Moon, Earth’s radio noise is blocked. Real missions fly halo orbits at Sun–Earth and Earth–Moon Lagrange points.
scenario.sandbox.name: Sandbox
scenario.sandbox.tagline: No budget, no deadline — just physics.
scenario.sandbox.objective: Build anything, fly it anywhere. There is no budget limit and no pass/fail; watch how every choice moves the resources.
scenario.sandbox.whyItMatters: Engineers prototype freely before a real mission constrains them.

investor.commercial.name: Commercial Partner

tech.rideshare.name: Rideshare contract
tech.rideshare.description: Book seats on shared flights to sun-synchronous orbit. Cheap per kg; fixed dates and altitude.
tech.reusable_medium.name: Reusable boosters (R-2)
tech.reusable_medium.description: First stages that land and fly again: ~40% cheaper launches, ~30% less payload.
tech.reusable_heavy.name: Reusable heavy (R-3)
tech.reusable_heavy.description: Three cores that land: heavy-lift capacity at a medium price. Opens fast routes to the Moon and L2.
tech.super_heavy.name: Fully reusable super-heavy + orbital refuelling
tech.super_heavy.description: In development in the real world. Coming in Act 3 (Moon and Mars).
tech.nuclear_stage.name: Nuclear-thermal upper stage
tech.nuclear_stage.description: Speculative: researched for decades, not operational. Act 4.
contract.first_light.title: First Light
contract.first_light.blurb: Fly Paulet-1, the sounding rocket you built from Paulet’s notebooks, past the 100 km line with a small experiment.
contract.earth_watch.title: Earth Watch
contract.earth_watch.blurb: Your first satellite: watch forests and farms for two years.
contract.andean_eye.title: Andean Eye
contract.andean_eye.blurb: Glaciers and forest edges of the Andes on a foundation budget.
contract.station_resupply.title: Station Resupply
contract.station_resupply.blurb: Carry a tonne of supplies to the space station. Reusable rockets shine here.
contract.storm_tracker.title: Storm Tracker
contract.storm_tracker.blurb: A geostationary weather watcher: far, expensive, irradiated.
contract.lunar_pathfinder.title: Lunar Pathfinder
contract.lunar_pathfinder.blurb: Act 2 begins: hunt for water ice at the lunar poles.
contract.lagrange_observatory.title: Lagrange Observatory
contract.lagrange_observatory.blurb: A telescope on a halo orbit around Earth–Moon L2 — where the three-body problem and chaos rule.
contract.mars_stranded.title: Stranded
contract.mars_stranded.blurb: An astronaut is stranded on Mars. Send supplies and a radio relay — the launch window will not wait.
contract.mars_stranded.note: Coming in Act 3: launch windows every ~26 months, 7–9 month trips, minutes of radio delay, entry–descent–landing.
contract.mars_oxygen.title: Breathing Mars
contract.mars_oxygen.blurb: Make oxygen from the Martian air, as a real rover experiment already did on a small scale.
contract.mars_oxygen.note: Coming in Act 3. Real reference: the MOXIE experiment on the Perseverance rover produced oxygen from CO₂ (2021–2023).
contract.mars_terraform.title: Terraforming (grand challenge)
contract.mars_terraform.blurb: Warm and thicken the Martian atmosphere over centuries — the dream at the end of the road.
contract.mars_terraform.note: Speculative. A 2018 NASA-supported study found too little accessible CO₂ to terraform Mars with today’s technology.
sim.slip.one: Launch slipped {months} month: the launcher had a ground-test anomaly.
sim.slip.other: Launch slipped {months} months: the launcher had a ground-test anomaly.
sim.launch.fail: Launch failure. The {launcher} did not reach orbit (≈{pct}% chance with this rocket).
sim.launch.ok: Launch successful on the {launcher}. Spacecraft separated and healthy.
sim.booster.landed: The first-stage booster landed and can fly again.
sim.booster.lost: The booster missed its landing and was lost at sea (the mission is fine; the next flight costs more).
sim.route: Route: {route}. Correction reserve on board: {reserve} m/s.
sim.tcm.ok: Course corrections used {need} of the {reserve} m/s reserve; {left} m/s kept for station-keeping.
sim.chaos.title: The trajectory drifted more than planned
sim.chaos.text: Tiny errors grew on the way (that is chaos): arriving needs {need} m/s of corrections, but the reserve was {reserve} m/s. Missing: {deficit} m/s.
sim.chaos.borrow.hintOk: The mission may end a little earlier.
sim.chaos.borrow.hintLow: Most of the station-keeping budget: the mission will be short.
sim.chaos.loose: Accept a wider, less stable orbit
sim.flare.title: Solar flare detected
sim.flare.text.hard: A strong flare is heading our way. Your {obc} is radiation-hardened. Keep observing, or hide in safe mode for two weeks?
sim.flare.text.soft: A strong flare is heading our way. Your {obc} is NOT radiation-hardened. Keep observing, or hide in safe mode for two weeks?
sim.flare.safe.hint: No science for 2 weeks; much less radiation damage.
sim.flare.continue.hintSoft: Risk a computer reset and extra radiation damage.
sim.battery.title: Battery cell failure
sim.battery.text: One battery cell failed: capacity is down ~20%. Each eclipse now drains {pct}% of the battery.
sim.battery.reduce.hint: Less science, but the battery ages normally.
sim.battery.accept.hintHigh: Battery will wear out much faster.
sim.station.title: Ground station offline
sim.station.text: {station} is down for {weeks} weeks (power failure). Rent time on a commercial backup antenna?
sim.station.rent.hint: No data loss; costs reserve money.
sim.station.wait.hintBad: Data will pile up and may be lost.
sim.station.wait.hintOk: Other stations can cover most of it.
sim.micrometeoroid: Micrometeoroid hit a solar array: −8% power.
sim.debris.title: Space debris conjunction
sim.debris.text.can: A dead satellite fragment will pass within 200 m in 36 hours (≈2% collision risk). Burn propellant to dodge?
sim.debris.text.cannot: A debris fragment will pass within 200 m (≈2% collision risk). You have no propellant to dodge.
sim.debris.burn.hint: Uses a little propellant, removes the risk.
sim.budget.title: Investors cut the budget
sim.budget.text: Your funders are cutting ${cut} M from operations. Reserve available: ${reserve} M.
sim.budget.absorb.hintLow: Reserve is too small: operations will stop early.
sim.budget.drop: Cancel the most expensive ground station
sim.opp.missed: {title} — missed: no suitable instrument on board ({names}).
sim.opp.retarget.hint: +{science} science; doubles data for one week.
sim.drift.title: Orbit drifting away from L2
sim.drift.text: Tracking shows the spacecraft slowly sliding off its halo orbit. In a chaotic orbit small deviations grow exponentially — correcting now is cheap, later it is not.
sim.drift.correct.hint: A small burn while the error is small.
sim.drift.wait.hint: Saves propellant if the drift reverses… but it usually grows.
sim.eclipse.coped: Lunar eclipse: {hours} h in Earth's shadow — the battery coped ({pct}% used).
sim.eclipse.title: Lunar eclipse ahead
sim.eclipse.text: The Moon will pass through Earth's shadow for hours. In safe mode the spacecraft still needs {pct}% of its battery.
sim.eclipse.precharge: Pre-charge and power down for a week
sim.eclipse.precharge.hint: Lose a week of science; best survival odds.
sim.eclipse.ride.hintFlat: Battery will run flat: spacecraft likely lost.
sim.eclipse.ride.hintDeep: Deep discharge will age the battery.
sim.do.flare.safe: {who}: safe mode during the flare. Radiation +0.5 krad.
sim.do.flare.reboot: {who} kept observing: the computer rebooted. 3 weeks to recover, {lost} GB of stored data lost.
sim.do.flare.kept: {who} kept observing through the flare. Radiation +{krad} krad.
sim.do.battery.reduce: {who}: duty cycles −20% to protect the battery.
sim.do.battery.accept: {who}: operating as planned with a weaker battery.
sim.do.station.wait: {who}: waiting for the station to come back.
sim.do.debris.burn: {who}: avoidance burn done. Debris passed safely.
sim.end.collision: Collision with space debris. The spacecraft is lost.
sim.do.debris.accept: {who} accepted the risk. The debris missed by 150 m.
sim.do.budget.absorb: {who} absorbed the ${cut} M cut from the reserve.
sim.do.chaos.borrow: {who} used {deficit} m/s of station-keeping propellant to reach the planned orbit.
sim.do.chaos.loose: {who} accepted a wider orbit: −25% science, propellant kept.
sim.do.drift.correct: {who}: correction burn done while the error was small (1.5 m/s).
sim.do.drift.grew: {who} waited: the drift grew exponentially and the correction cost 6 m/s.
sim.do.drift.lucky: {who} waited and the drift happened to reverse. Lucky this time.
sim.do.eclipse.precharge: {who}: pre-charged and powered down. Survived the eclipse.
sim.end.eclipse: The battery ran flat in Earth’s shadow. The spacecraft froze and was lost.
sim.do.eclipse.ride: {who} rode it out. Deep discharge aged the battery.
sim.end.radiation: Radiation dose reached {dose} krad: the {obc} failed.
sim.end.power: Solar arrays can no longer power the spacecraft. Mission over.
sim.end.funding: The money ran out: investors stopped funding operations.
sim.end.battery: The battery is worn out and can no longer survive eclipses.
sim.end.propellant: Out of propellant: the orbit can no longer be maintained.
sim.end.decayed: Without thrusters the orbit decayed. Mission over.

scenario.earth_watch.opportunity.title: Fire season over the Amazon
scenario.earth_watch.opportunity.text: Smoke plumes are rising over the southern Amazon. Retargeting now could map burn scars and vegetation stress — but it will flood the downlink for a week.
scenario.lunar_pathfinder.opportunity.ti: Fresh impact near the south pole
scenario.lunar_pathfinder.opportunity.te: A small meteorite just hit the Moon near a shadowed crater, exposing fresh material. Pointing everything at it this week could reveal buried ice.
scenario.andean_eye.opportunity.title: Glacial lake warning
scenario.andean_eye.opportunity.text: A glacial lake above a mountain town is swelling fast. Imaging it every pass this week could give the authorities an early warning.
scenario.storm_tracker.opportunity.title: Rapid intensification
scenario.storm_tracker.opportunity.text: A tropical storm is exploding into a major hurricane. Rapid-scan imaging every few minutes would help forecasters — and fill the downlink.
scenario.lagrange_observatory.opportunit: A supernova in a nearby galaxy
A star just exploded in a nearby galaxy. Pointing the telescope at it for a week would capture its infrared glow while it lasts.
route.lunar_polar.direct.name: Direct transfer (~5 days)
route.lunar_polar.direct.description: Fast and well understood, but you arrive fast too: a big braking burn to be captured.
route.lunar_polar.direct.realWorld: Most lunar orbiters and all Apollo missions took a few days on a direct trajectory.
route.lunar_polar.low_energy.name: Low-energy transfer (~3.5 months)
route.lunar_polar.low_energy.description: A long loop far beyond the Moon where the Sun’s and Earth’s pull do part of the braking for you. Saves propellant, costs months and needs careful corrections.
route.lunar_polar.low_energy.realWorld: NASA’s GRAIL twins (2011) reached the Moon after a low-energy transfer of about three and a half months.
route.em_l2_halo.direct.name: Direct transfer (~1 week)
route.em_l2_halo.direct.realWorld: Direct transfers to lunar halo orbits take about a week but need a large insertion burn.
route.em_l2_halo.flyby.name: Lunar flyby assist (~3 weeks)
route.em_l2_halo.flyby.description: Swing past the Moon so its gravity bends and slows your path — a gravity assist.
route.em_l2_halo.flyby.realWorld: Gravity assists let probes change speed and direction without propellant (e.g. lunar swing-bys of several missions).
route.em_l2_halo.low_energy.name: Ballistic low-energy transfer (~4 months)
route.em_l2_halo.low_energy.description: Ride the gravitational “highways” of the Sun–Earth–Moon system. Very little propellant, but four months of travel through chaotic territory.
route.em_l2_halo.low_energy.realWorld: The CAPSTONE cubesat (2022) took about four months on a ballistic lunar transfer to reach its near-rectilinear halo orbit.
investor.agency.wants: Science and safety. Dislikes failures and risk.
investor.commercial.wants: Delivery on time and on budget. Pays per result.
investor.foundation.wants: Impact on people and the planet. Patient with small budgets.
intro.caption.1: On a rooftop beneath the Misti volcano,
intro.caption.2: a kid kept asking the same question:
intro.caption.3: how do you get up there?
intro.caption.4: The first answer came from this same land.
intro.caption.5: Pedro Paulet, an engineer who, according to his own account,
intro.caption.6: tested a liquid-fuel rocket engine in Paris in the 1890s.
intro.caption.7: That kid grew up to be a physicist.
rocket.title: Rocket workbench
rocket.subtitle: Build a launcher from engines, tanks and boosters. Every part moves the numbers on the right: mass, thrust-to-weight and Δv.
rocket.stages.hint: Stage 1 lifts off; each stage above fires after the one below drops away. Dropping empty tanks is why rockets have stages.
rocket.stage.stats: Full {wet} t ({prop} t of propellant) · Δv {dv} m/s
rocket.engine.stats: Thrust {sl} kN at sea level, {vac} kN in vacuum · Isp {isp} s
rocket.boosters.hint: Solid boosters add a lot of thrust at liftoff and drop away when empty. They come in pairs to keep the rocket balanced.
rocket.fairing.hint: The nose cover that protects the spacecraft through the air. The spacecraft must fit inside; it is dropped with the first stage.
rocket.recovery.hint: Landing legs and grid fins let the first stage land and fly again: cheaper flights, but the landing propellant is payload you do not carry.
rocket.drawing: Side view of your rocket, to scale
rocket.view3d.label: 3D model of your rocket, to scale
rocket.view3d.hint: Drag to turn it. The blue figure is a person, 1.8 m tall.
rocket.reusable: Reusable first stage · lands {pct}% of the time
rocket.expendable: Expendable: thrown away after each flight
rocket.capacity.hint: The largest payload that still reaches each target, also limited by liftoff thrust and the fairing. The bar shows how far your Δv with the test payload gets.
rocket.target.need: needs {dv} m/s, including gravity and drag losses
rocket.ok.title: Ready to fly
rocket.ok.why: No problems found with this design.
rocket.issue.ROCKET_INCOMPLETE.title: The rocket is incomplete
rocket.issue.ROCKET_INCOMPLETE.why: Every stage needs an engine and a tank, and the rocket needs a fairing.
rocket.issue.ROCKET_FUEL_MISMATCH.title: Stage {stage}: engine and tank do not match
rocket.issue.ROCKET_FUEL_MISMATCH.why: The {engine} cannot burn what the {tank} holds. Pick a tank with the engine’s propellant.
A vacuum engine cannot lift off
The {engine} has a long nozzle made for space; at sea level the air pressure stops it from working. Use a sea-level engine on the first stage.
rocket.issue.ROCKET_SEA_LEVEL_UPPER.titl: Sea-level engine on an upper stage
rocket.issue.ROCKET_SEA_LEVEL_UPPER.why: Upper stages fire in vacuum, where a vacuum nozzle gives more Isp. A vacuum engine would add Δv.
rocket.issue.ROCKET_LEGS_NO_FINS.title: Legs without grid fins
rocket.issue.ROCKET_LEGS_NO_FINS.why: Without fins the stage cannot steer back to the landing ship. Add grid fins, or remove the legs to save mass.
rocket.issue.ROCKET_ENGINE_NO_RESTART.ti: This engine cannot relight to land
rocket.issue.ROCKET_ENGINE_NO_RESTART.wh: The {engine} cannot restart for the landing burn, so the first stage cannot come back. Use a restartable engine such as the K-8 or the M-20.
rocket.issue.ROCKET_TWR_LOW.title: Too heavy to lift off
rocket.issue.ROCKET_TWR_LOW.why: Thrust-to-weight at liftoff is {twr}: the engines push less than the rocket weighs. Add engines or boosters, or carry less propellant.
rocket.issue.ROCKET_TWR_MARGINAL.title: Barely lifts off
rocket.issue.ROCKET_TWR_MARGINAL.why: Thrust-to-weight is {twr}. A slow climb wastes propellant fighting gravity (gravity losses). Aim for 1.2 to 2.
rocket.issue.ROCKET_TWR_HIGH.title: More thrust than needed
rocket.issue.ROCKET_TWR_HIGH.why: Thrust-to-weight is {twr}. Engines are heavy and expensive, and a fast climb through thick air adds drag. Fewer engines would do.
rocket.issue.ROCKET_UPPER_TWR_LOW.title: Stage {stage} pushes too gently
rocket.issue.ROCKET_UPPER_TWR_LOW.why: Its thrust-to-weight is {twr}: it would burn for a very long time while gravity pulls it down. Add an engine or carry less propellant.
rocket.issue.ROCKET_NO_ORBIT.title: Cannot reach orbit
rocket.issue.ROCKET_NO_ORBIT.why: With no payload this rocket gives {dv} m/s, but low Earth orbit needs about {need} m/s (including gravity and drag losses). Add a stage, more propellant or more efficient engines.
rocket.issue.ROCKET_FAIRING_SMALL.title: The payload does not fit
rocket.issue.ROCKET_FAIRING_SMALL.why: The test payload is {payload} kg; this fairing fits up to {max} kg. Choose a bigger fairing.
rocketPart.k_small.name: Small kerosene engine (K-1)
rocketPart.k_small.description: A small pump-fed engine. Nine of them lift a light rocket.
rocketPart.k_small_vac.name: Small vacuum kerosene engine (K-1V)
rocketPart.k_small_vac.description: A long nozzle for space: more efficient, but it cannot fire at sea level.
rocketPart.k_med.name: Kerosene engine (K-8)
rocketPart.k_med.description: The workhorse of medium rockets. It can relight to land a booster.
rocketPart.k_med_vac.name: Vacuum kerosene engine (K-8V)
rocketPart.k_med_vac.description: Upper-stage version with a large nozzle for the vacuum of space.
rocketPart.m_big.name: Methane engine (M-20)
rocketPart.m_big.description: Burns methane and oxygen: clean, efficient and made to fly again and again.
rocketPart.m_vac.name: Vacuum methane engine (M-20V)
rocketPart.m_vac.description: Methane engine with a vacuum nozzle for upper stages.
rocketPart.h_main.name: Hydrogen main engine (H-200)
rocketPart.h_main.description: Liquid hydrogen gives the best efficiency of any chemical engine, but the fuel is bulky and the engine expensive.
rocketPart.h_upper.name: Hydrogen upper engine (H-10)
rocketPart.h_upper.description: Small, very efficient upper-stage engine: the classic choice to reach high orbits and the Moon.
rocketPart.srb_s.name: Small solid booster (S-20)
rocketPart.srb_s.description: Strap-on solid motor: lots of thrust at liftoff, cannot be switched off.
rocketPart.srb_l.name: Large solid booster (S-150)
rocketPart.srb_l.description: A big solid motor for heavy rockets: it does the hardest part of the climb.
